Bootstrap linear regression

Sebastian Ross

2026-09-12

1 Introduction

Today we are going to look at the a group of stroke predictors. We are looking to predict strokes with them being one of the leading cause of death. We are looking to fide if a person will have a stroke and what are the strongest predictor of strokes. We will be doing linear regression to find linear relationships and explore how the bootstraps method can enhance our linear regression.

url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Kingsoul42/STA-321/main/dataset/healthcare-dataset-stroke-data.csv"

stroke_predictions <- read.csv(url, header = TRUE)

var.name <- names(stroke_predictions)
kable(data.frame(var.name))
var.name
id
gender
age
hypertension
heart_disease
ever_married
work_type
Residence_type
avg_glucose_level
bmi
smoking_status
stroke

2 Materials

This data set is collected by the world health organization trying to predict if a person is going to have a stroke based on various factors.They are trying to predict strokes because they are the second leading cause of death. id, gender, age, hypertension, heart_disease, ever_married, work_type, Residence_type, avg_glucose_level, bmi, smoking_status, and stroke are the variables that we are examining. some of the issues could be that for simple linear regression with there being a bunch of categorical variables with more than 2 levels meaning we can’t use simple linear regreassion. Age, avg_glucose_level, and bmi are the only numeric values that can be used for anylisis given the id is only a way to know which observation we ar looking at. The other variables are categorical variables with most of them having more than 2 categories which we cannot use for this analysis with it looking at numaric variables that are not toggles.

pairs.panels(stroke_predictions[, c(3,9,10)], pch=21, main="Pair-wise Scatter Plot of r numerical variables")

age <- stroke_predictions$age
avg_glucose_level <- stroke_predictions$avg_glucose_level
plot(age, avg_glucose_level, pch = 21, col ="navy",
     main = "Relationship between Distance and Price")

parametric.model <- lm(  age~avg_glucose_level)
par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(parametric.model)

3 Methodology and Analysis

Looking at some of the above graphs we see that age and avg_glucouse_level as a roughly linear relation so I decided to look at their relationship. but when we look at the residual graphs we see some issues with the graphs that go against model assumption. In the top left we see the line has a slight curve and having a weird point clustering into groups. We also see that there seems to be a hard ceiling and a pattern with the shape sloping down. For the top right we see that the points should be straight line but ours is a bit of an s shape with point veering off especially at the top. This shows that the data does not follow the normality assumption. The bottom left graph shows that we have non constant variance as our fitted values get larger. While the bottom right pot shows that we have some influential outliers with values being above hooks distance.

lambda = 1/4
avg_glucose_level.25 = (avg_glucose_level^lambda-1)/lambda
boxcox.m = lm(avg_glucose_level.25 ~ age)
##
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(boxcox.m)

4 Transformations

With the bos cox transformation that we used to attemt to fix these issues with the model assumption. The top left is flatter but their seems to be a hard floot to how low the values can be. The top right is made worse by the bos cox transformation meaning it did not fix the non-normality issue we were having. Now the bottom left is now sloped upwards instead of downwards but there still seems to be a bit of a pattern with more clustering on the right and a bit of a pattern. Now for the bottom right it did fix the observations from crossing hooks distance making the outliers less influential. With these it looks like we will need to use a non-parametric test like the bootstrap regression that doesn’t have the same model assumptions.

vec.id <- 1:length(age)   # vector of observation ID
boot.id <- sample(vec.id, length(age), replace = TRUE)   # bootstrap obs ID.
boot.age <- age[boot.id]           # bootstrap price
boot.avg_glucose_level <- avg_glucose_level[boot.id]
boot.beta0 <- NULL    # rep(0,1000)
boot.beta1 <- NULL    
## bootstrap regression models using for-loop
vec.id <- 1:length(age)   # vector of observation ID
for(i in 1:1000){
  boot.id <- sample(vec.id, length(age), replace = TRUE)   # bootstrap obs ID.
  boot.age <- age[boot.id]           # bootstrap price
  boot.avg_glucose_level <- avg_glucose_level[boot.id]     # corresponding bootstrap alucose
  ## regression
  boot.reg <-lm(age[boot.id] ~ avg_glucose_level[boot.id]) 
  boot.beta0[i] <- coef(boot.reg)[1]   # bootstrap intercept
  boot.beta1[i] <- coef(boot.reg)[2]
}
boot.beta0.ci <- quantile(boot.beta0, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 2)
boot.beta1.ci <- quantile(boot.beta1, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 2)
boot.coef <- data.frame(rbind(boot.beta0.ci, boot.beta1.ci)) 
names(boot.coef) <- c("2.5%", "97.5%")
kable(boot.coef, caption = "Bootstrap 95% Confidence Intervals for Beta Coefficients")
Bootstrap 95% Confidence Intervals for Beta Coefficients
2.5% 97.5%
boot.beta0.ci 29.2074122 32.0013526
boot.beta1.ci 0.1077562 0.1296029

5 Results and Conclusions

From all the plots and graphs we see that there were violations to model assumptions. We especially violated normality, constant variance, as well as groupings as we can see from the residual plots. With this we use the bootstrap non-parametric method to try and not need the model assumption. Some of the groupings of the plots makes sense given it is impossible for you to have a 0 average glucose level. From the bootstrap method we see that (0.108 0.13) we see that both are positive meaning they are positively correlated. These seem to show that both are significantly different from 0 meaning showing they are both significant. (0.108 0.13) increase every 1 year in age and it is not till 29.2074122 or 32.0013526 where glucose starts to be factored in. In this case I would use the bootstrap as there are to many model assumptions broken for the simple linear regression model to be used.Even with the transformation we cannot use simple linear regression because the model assumption are still broken. Meaning we would need to use a non-parametric method such of the bootstrap.
